title: PhenoFuse 4.0.4 - VNIR reflectance check and empirical calibration
Is my hyperspectral cube reflectance or radiance, and how to fix it in the tool

PhenoFuse four point zero point four. This video shows how to check whether a VNIR hyperspectral cube is reflectance or radiance, and how to correct a radiance cube with the empirical line calibration built into the tool.
why: Radiance = light that arrived at the sensor (sun x surface x atmosphere) · Reflectance = the surface alone (0-1)

First, the difference. Radiance is the light that arrived at the sensor: sunlight, times the surface, times the atmosphere. Reflectance is the surface alone, a fraction between zero and one. A radiance cube still carries the sun's absorption lines at seven hundred and sixty and nine hundred and forty nanometres, and near infrared is about equal to red, so every vegetation index is meaningless. All PhenoFuse VNIR features assume reflectance.
tab: Reflectance check and empirical calibration group, below the inputs

Open the VNIR Spectral Features tab. Below the inputs there is a new group, reflectance check and empirical calibration. It has a check button, a reference choice, the reference inputs, the soil N D V I limit, and the calibrate button.
check_rad: Pick the cube → the check runs → RADIANCE in red, with the numbers behind the verdict

Pick the VNIR cube. The check runs automatically, and the check cube button repeats it. Here the result is radiance, in red: the oxygen dip at seven sixty nanometres is zero point seven two of its flanks, the water vapour dip zero point five three, N I R over red is one, and the N D V I median is zero. A warning explains that every index on this cube would be meaningless. The first choice is always to reprocess the flight to reflectance; when that is not possible, use the calibration below.
targets: 3 · Reference option A: targets in this flight
Panel or tarp polygons + their reflectance spectrum (CSV) · same date, same light · 2+ targets also fit an offset

Reference option A is the proper empirical line: a calibration panel or tarp photographed in the same flight. You give the tool the polygons of the targets and their reflectance spectrum as a C S V. One target gives a gain per band; two or more targets of different brightness also fit an offset per band.
csv: wavelength_nm + one column per target (reflectance 0-1) · any step, interpolated to the cube's bands

Where does the spectrum come from? Best is the panel's calibration certificate, which lists reflectance against wavelength; the panel used by the GRYFN processing has one. Second, a field spectroradiometer measurement of the tarp, ideally on the flight day. Third, a nominal value for a grey flat panel, entered as a number in the polygon's refl column. The C S V has a wavelength column in nanometres and one reflectance column per target, at any wavelength step; the tool interpolates to the cube's bands.
qgis: Preparing the target polygons in QGIS
New Shapefile Layer · Polygon · CRS of the cube · fields name (text) and refl (decimal) · digitise inside the panel

The polygons are drawn in QGIS. Create a new shapefile layer, polygon geometry, in the cube's coordinate system, with two fields: name, text, and refl, decimal. Digitise one polygon per target well inside the panel, away from its edges, shadows and glint. Set name to the matching C S V column, or refl to the nominal value when there is no spectrum. Save it, then pick the shapefile under target polygons and the C S V under target spectra.
refcube: 4 · Reference option B: a calibrated cube of the same trial
Bare soil (reference NDVI < 0.20: tracks and alleys) as the invariant target · same day best, other date with caveats

Reference option B is for flights without a panel: a calibrated reflectance cube of the same trial. The bare soil of the trial, where the reference N D V I is below the limit, that is the wheel tracks and alleys, becomes the invariant target. The gain per band is the median reference reflectance over those positions divided by the median value of this cube at the same positions. A calibrated flight of the same day is nearly exact. Another date assumes the soil did not change: ratio indices stay reliable, absolute reflectance is uncertain by ten to twenty percent. Here the reference is the September flight of the same trial.
calibrate: Samples both cubes · gain per band · writes <cube>_reflectance_empirical.bin on the same grid

Press calibrate. The tool samples both cubes at the same map positions, derives the gain per band, and writes the calibrated cube next to the original as an E N V I file on the same grid, reflectance times ten thousand, with the wavelengths in the header. It also writes the gain table, a README with the recipe and caveats, a J S O N with the diagnostics, and a before and after figure.
calib_done: Samples, bare-soil count, gain repeatability between two halves, verdict before and after

The summary reports the samples used, the number of bare soil positions, the repeatability of the gain between two halves of the samples, and the verdict before and after. The cube field now points to the calibrated cube.
qa: Left: spectrum before, with the absorption dips · middle: the gain curve · right: spectrum after, crop pixels of the reference against the same pixels calibrated

Open the Q A figure. On the left, the spectrum before, with the two absorption dips. In the middle, the gain curve: it must be smooth, with peaks only at seven sixty and nine forty nanometres where it undoes the absorption. On the right, the spectrum after, and for a cube reference the crop pixels of the reference against the same pixels after calibration. If the repeatability is worse than a few percent or the curve is ragged, the reference was too small or not invariant: raise the soil N D V I limit or use a different reference.
check_ok: Check again → REFLECTANCE in green, dips gone, NIR/red above 1.2
Run the check again on the calibrated cube. It now reads reflectance, in green: the dips are gone and N I R over red is above one point two.
features: VNIR features per plot on the corrected grid · provenance records the calibrated cube and the method

Finally run the VNIR features per plot as usual, on the corrected grid. The provenance file records the calibrated cube and the method, so the dataset keeps its audit trail. Treat ratio indices as reliable; treat absolute reflectance from a cross-date soil reference as approximate.
outro: Check → choose the reference → calibrate → verify → extract · fly a tarp and keep its certificate with the project

To summarise: check the cube, choose the reference, calibrate, verify, and extract. Fly a reference tarp on every campaign and keep its certificate with the project, and the correction becomes a two minute step with no cross date assumption. The full guidance is on the Guidance tab under reflectance check and empirical calibration.
